request.instructions: You are a single agent working alone. Solve the task directly and completely. State your final answer explicitly on the last line, prefixed with 'Answer:'.

messages.content: Produce a rigorous technical brief on optimizing compiler internals. For EACH of the following areas you must discuss at least three specific named mechanisms in real depth: (1) SSA construction, (2) alias analysis, (3) register allocation, (4) inlining, (5) escape analysis, (6) loop vectorization, (7) instruction scheduling, (8) loop optimizations . Use precise standard terminology for every mechanism you name. Be exhaustive: a shallow mention of an area does not count as covering it.

response.content:
# Technical Brief: Optimizing Compiler Internals

## 1. SSA Construction

**Cytron et al.'s dominance-frontier algorithm.** The classical method for converting a CFG into Static Single Assignment form proceeds in two phases: φ-placement and variable renaming. For each variable v, φ-functions are inserted at the iterated dominance frontier DF⁺(Defs(v)) — the dominance frontier DF(n) of a node n being the set of CFG nodes w such that n dominates a predecessor of w but does not strictly dominate w itself. Computing dominance frontiers requires the dominator tree, typically built with the **Lengauer–Tarjan algorithm** (semidominators plus path compression, near-linear O(E α(E,N))) or the simpler **Cooper–Harvey–Kennedy iterative data-flow algorithm**, which intersects dominator sets by walking up the dominator tree using postorder numbers and is faster in practice on real CFGs despite worse asymptotic bounds. The renaming phase then performs a preorder walk of the dominator tree with a per-variable stack of reaching definitions, rewriting uses and filling φ-operands along each CFG edge.

**Pruned and semi-pruned SSA.** Vanilla ("minimal") SSA places φ-functions even for variables dead at the join point. *Pruned SSA* runs a liveness analysis first and inserts a φ for v at block b only if v is live-in at b, minimizing φ count at the cost of a full live-variable analysis. *Semi-pruned SSA* (Briggs et al.) is the engineering compromise: it computes the set of "non-local" names — variables live across basic-block boundaries, detected cheaply in one pass by tracking block-local kills — and only inserts φs for those, skipping liveness. LLVM's `mem2reg`/`PromoteMemToReg` pass effectively builds pruned SSA by promoting alloca slots and using block-level liveness to suppress dead φs, with fast paths for variables defined in a single block (single-store case uses dominance directly, no φs at all).

**Braun et al.'s simple-and-efficient on-the-fly construction.** Braun, Buchwald, Hack et al. (CC 2013) construct SSA directly while generating IR from an AST, without a prior CFG, dominator tree, or dominance frontiers. The core operations are `writeVariable(var, block, value)` and `readVariable(var, block)`: a read in a block with a local definition returns it; otherwise *global value numbering–style* recursive lookup walks predecessors, inserting operandless φs in blocks that are not yet "sealed" (i.e., whose predecessor set may still grow), completing them when the block is sealed. Trivial φs (all operands equal or self-referential) are removed eagerly, which, with on-the-fly removal plus a final SCC-based cleanup (per Aycock–Horspool-style redundancy removal), yields minimal SSA on reducible CFGs. This is the approach used in Go's gc compiler frontend-adjacent construction and in libFirm. Related forms worth naming: **SSI (Static Single Information)** and **block arguments** (MLIR/Swift SIL replace φ-nodes with basic-block parameters, which is isomorphic to SSA but avoids φ ordering/parallel-copy ambiguities), and **destruction** via Sreedhar's Method III or Boissinot et al.'s liveness-based parallel-copy lowering to leave conventional SSA (CSSA) before register allocation.

## 2. Alias Analysis

**Andersen's inclusion-based (subset-based) points-to analysis.** Formulated as set-inclusion constraints over points-to sets: `p = &x` yields x ∈ pts(p); `p = q` yields pts(q) ⊆ pts(p); `*p = q` and `p = *q` generate complex constraints resolved iteratively. Solved as dynamic transitive closure over a constraint graph; worst case O(n³). Scalability comes from **cycle elimination** (Fähndrich et al.'s partial online cycle detection, Hardekopf–Lin's *Lazy Cycle Detection* and *Hybrid Cycle Detection*) which collapses strongly connected components of pointer-equivalent nodes, plus **offline variable substitution** and BDD- or bitmap-based points-to set representations. Flow-insensitive and (usually) context-insensitive; precision can be recovered with context sensitivity (k-CFA / call-strings, or object sensitivity in JVMs) at exponential cost.

**Steensgaard's unification-based analysis.** Almost-linear time (O(n α(n))) using union-find: every assignment `p = q` *unifies* the points-to equivalence classes of p and q rather than making one a subset of the other. The type system interpretation treats each abstract location as having a single points-to "type," merged on constraint. Far less precise than Andersen (asymmetric assignments collapse distinct targets) but so cheap it's usable as a prefilter or in JIT settings; it underlies early GCC points-to work and many fast whole-program analyses.

**Type-based alias analysis (TBAA) and compiler rule-based disambiguation.** TBAA (Diwan, McKinley, Moss) exploits language typing rules: in C/C++ "strict aliasing," an lvalue of type T may not alias an object of unrelated effective type, so an `int*` store cannot modify a `float` object. LLVM encodes this as `!tbaa` metadata forming a type DAG with access-path (struct-path) refinement; GCC implements it via alias sets consulted in `-fstrict-aliasing` mode. Complementary named mechanisms in production: **LLVM BasicAA**, a stateless rule-based analyzer combining distinct-globals/allocas reasoning, `noalias`/`restrict` attributes (the C99 `restrict` qualifier formalized), GEP (getelementptr) arithmetic decomposition with constant-offset disambiguation, and escape/capture analysis of allocas; **ScopedNoAliasAA** for inlined restrict scopes; and **shape/field-sensitive analyses** such as SVF's flow-sensitive sparse analysis built on memory SSA. For loop dependence specifically, array disambiguation uses the **GCD test, Banerjee inequalities, and the Omega test** (Pugh's integer programming over Presburger formulas) — these are dependence tests layered atop base alias facts.

## 3. Register Allocation

**Chaitin–Briggs graph coloring.** Build an *interference graph* (nodes = live ranges, edges = simultaneous liveness), then apply Kempe-style simplification: repeatedly remove nodes with degree < k (k = number of registers), pushing them on a stack; if stuck, choose a *spill candidate* by cost/degree heuristic. Chaitin spilled eagerly ("pessimistic"); **Briggs's optimistic coloring** instead pushes high-degree nodes anyway and only spills if no color is actually available at pop time, which colors many graphs Chaitin rejects (e.g., diamond interference patterns). Integral sub-mechanisms: **coalescing** of move-related ranges — Chaitin's aggressive coalescing vs. **Briggs's conservative coalescing** (coalesce only if the merged node has < k high-degree neighbors) and **George's iterated coalescing** criterion (every neighbor of a either interferes with b or has insignificant degree), unified in George–Appel *iterated register coalescing*; **live-range splitting**; **rematerialization** (recompute never-spill values like constants instead of reloading, per Briggs–Cooper–Torczon); and spill-code insertion with Bernstein-style spill-cost metrics.

**Linear scan and second-chance binpacking.** Poletto–Sarkar linear scan sorts live *intervals* by start point and allocates greedily, maintaining an active list and spilling the interval with the furthest end when registers are exhausted — O(n log n), ideal for JITs (early HotSpot client, V8 baseline tiers). **Traub et al.'s second-chance binpacking** and Wimmer–Franz's **linear scan on SSA with interval splitting** refine this: lifetime holes are exploited, intervals can be split at arbitrary positions, and use-position weights guide eviction. **LLVM's Greedy Register Allocator** (RAGreedy) is the modern descendant: priority-queue–driven assignment over live intervals with eviction (dequeue by spill weight, may evict lighter intervals), *global and local live-range splitting* guided by edge-frequency (region splitting via spill placement/Hopfield-style cost model), last-chance recoloring, and deferred spilling — not a pure linear scan, but interval-based rather than full graph coloring.

**SSA-based allocation and PBQP.** Hack–Goos observed that interference graphs of programs *in SSA form* are **chordal**, hence optimally colorable in polynomial time by maximum-cardinality-search/perfect-elimination ordering; spilling is then decoupled ("spill first, color second") and performed before coloring (e.g., Belady/MIN-style furthest-use spilling per Braun–Hack), with SSA destruction/parallel-copy coalescing afterward. This underlies libFirm's allocator. **PBQP (Partitioned Boolean Quadratic Programming)** allocation (Scholz–Eckstein) encodes register assignment, irregular register classes, register pairs, and coalescing as cost matrices between variable nodes, solved by reduction rules (R0–R2 exact, RN heuristic); LLVM ships a PBQP allocator used for targets with irregular constraints.

## 4. Inlining

**Bottom-up call-graph inlining with cost/benefit heuristics (LLVM inliner).** LLVM's inliner walks SCCs of the call graph bottom-up (CGSCC pass manager) so callees are simplified before their callers consider them. The **InlineCost** analysis simulates the callee under the call site's actual arguments: constant arguments trigger simplification (branches folded, SROA-able allocas credited via an SROA savings bonus), and the resulting cost is compared against a threshold adjusted by call-site hotness (**profile-guided inlining**: PGO hotness multiplies thresholds; cold sites get `inlinecold-threshold`), `inlinehint`/`alwaysinline`/`noinline` attributes, and a vector/last-call bonuses. Deferred inlining and the ML-based replacement (**MLGO inlining-for-size policy**) are named production variants.

**Partial inlining and outlining-based splitting.** When a function has a cheap early-exit guard before an expensive body, **partial inlining** (LLVM's PartialInliner, Hot/Cold splitting in GCC via function splitting, `-freorder-blocks-and-partition` adjacent machinery) outlines the cold region into a separate function and inlines only the hot header, capturing the common fast path without code-size blowup. Related: **function cloning / IPCP-driven specialization** (GCC's `ipa-cp` with cloning; LLVM FunctionSpecialization) creates per-call-site specialized bodies when a parameter is constant, an alternative to inlining that preserves sharing.

**Speculative/guarded devirtualization and inline caching.** For indirect and virtual calls, **indirect-call promotion** uses value profiles (or class-hierarchy analysis, CHA, per Dean–Grove–Chambers) to insert a guard `if (fp == &likely_target)` and inline the likely target, with the slow path falling back to the indirect call. In JITs this is **polymorphic inline caching** (Hölzle–Chambers–Ungar, Self/V8/HotSpot): monomorphic→polymorphic→megamorphic cache states feed type feedback into the inliner, and **deoptimization** (uncommon traps in HotSpot, per Hölzle's dynamic deoptimization) lets the JIT inline speculatively under invalidation guards — class-hierarchy-based CHA inlining in HotSpot is invalidated on class loading. Must-name supporting machinery: the **open-world vs. closed-world (LTO/WPO)** distinction, and tail-duplication interaction with inlining in trace-based JITs.

## 5. Escape Analysis

**Choi et al.'s connection-graph analysis (IBM, Java).** Builds a *connection graph* per method with object nodes, reference nodes, and points-to/deferred/field edges; abstract escape states form a lattice — **GlobalEscape** (reachable from statics/thread objects), **ArgEscape** (reachable from arguments, i.e., escapes the method but not the thread), **NoEscape**. Interprocedural summarization maps callee connection graphs into callers. NoEscape objects become candidates for **stack allocation** and thread-local treatment; ArgEscape still permits **lock elision** (synchronization removal) if the object never becomes thread-visible.

**Kotzmann–Mössenböck / HotSpot C2 partial escape analysis and scalar replacement.** HotSpot C2 performs flow-sensitive EA over its sea-of-nodes IR; non-escaping allocations undergo **scalar replacement of aggregates** — the object is deconstructed into its fields held in registers, the allocation removed entirely (stronger than stack allocation). Stadler–Würthinger–Mössenböck's **Partial Escape Analysis** (Graal) virtualizes allocations along each control-flow path and *materializes* the object lazily only on branches where it actually escapes, moving allocation into cold paths and keeping the hot path allocation-free; requires deoptimization metadata so virtual objects can be rematerialized at uncommon-trap exits.

**Go's gc escape analysis.** A whole-package, data-flow analysis over an abstract assignment graph with edge weights representing dereference/address-of counts (the "≤ one level of indirection" shortest-path formulation in the current implementation, replacing the older exponential analysis): if a value's address flows to the heap (returned, stored to a sunk location, captured by an escaping closure, sent on a channel, or too large/variable-sized for the stack), it is heap-allocated; otherwise stack-allocated, reported via `-gcflags=-m`. Interacts with inlining (non-inlined calls force conservative parameter escape via `//go:noescape`-annotated exceptions in runtime/asm). Also nameable in this family: **region inference** (Tofte–Talpin, MLKit) as the type-system-based ancestor, and .NET RyuJIT's object stack allocation driven by a Choi-style analysis.

## 6. Loop Vectorization

**Classical loop vectorization with dependence analysis (Allen–Kennedy framework).** Legality rests on the **data-dependence graph** with distance/direction vectors: a loop-carried dependence with distance d < VF forbids naive vectorization. Named tests: **GCD test**, **Banerjee test**, **Omega test** (exact Presburger), and the **delta test** batching in production (LLVM DependenceAnalysis). Allen–Kennedy **codegen via loop distribution**: compute SCCs of the dependence graph, distribute the loop around them, vectorize the acyclic pieces, keep cyclic SCCs sequential; enabling transforms include **loop interchange** (to move a vectorizable dimension innermost, legal if the direction-vector permutation stays lexicographically positive) and **statement reordering**. Cyclic dependences that are **reductions** (sum/min/max recognized as reassociable recurrences) or **inductions** are handled specially via reduction variable expansion and horizontal/tree reduction epilogues; **if-conversion** turns control dependence into data dependence (predication/masking/select) so conditional bodies vectorize.

**LLVM Loop Vectorizer (VPlan) mechanics.** Innermost-loop vectorizer with: **runtime pointer aliasing checks** (memcheck versioning: emit overlap checks and branch to scalar loop on conflict) and SCEV predicate versioning; **vectorization factor (VF) and interleave count (IC) selection** via the cost model (now VPlan-based, including **scalable vectors** for SVE/RVV with `vscale`); **gather/scatter** and masked load/store emission for non-unit strides under predication; **interleaved access groups** (strided loads combined via shuffles); **tail folding by masking** (fold the scalar epilogue into the vector body with an active-lane mask) vs. scalar epilogue + **epilogue vectorization**; first-order recurrence vectorization; and search for the **SLP** complement. GCC's counterpart: the tree-vectorizer with its own versioning-for-alias/alignment and **loop peeling for alignment**.

**SLP (Superword-Level Parallelism) vectorization.** Larsen–Amarasinghe's SLP packs *isomorphic independent scalar statements* within a basic block into vector instructions: seed from adjacent memory accesses (or stores/reductions in LLVM's bottom-up SLP), grow packs through use-def chains building a vectorizable tree, cost-model the packing (including shuffle/insert/extract overhead), and emit vector code. **Loop-aware SLP** (unroll-and-SLP, Rosen et al. in GCC) unrolls a loop by VF and lets SLP pack across iterations — equivalent in power to loop vectorization for straight-line bodies. Also name: **outer-loop vectorization** (VPlan native path), and **polyhedral-model vectorization** (Polly/ISL scheduling for vectorizability as a scheduling objective).

## 7. Instruction Scheduling

**List scheduling over the data-dependence DAG.** The workhorse local scheduler: build a DAG of instructions in a basic block with edges weighted by latencies (true/anti/output dependences; memory edges from alias analysis), compute **critical-path length / height and depth priorities**, and greedily issue from a *ready list* each cycle respecting a machine resource model (reservation tables / scoreboards; in LLVM, **MachineScheduler (MISched)** with per-subtarget **SchedModel/itineraries**, bidirectional top-down/bottom-up queues, and **register-pressure tracking** heuristics like SethiUllman-style pressure sets to arbitrate between ILP and spills; pre-RA vs. post-RA scheduling both named). NP-hard in general; heuristics (maximum height, earliest start, resource hazards) dominate.

**Trace scheduling and superblock scheduling.** Fisher's **trace scheduling** picks the most probable acyclic path (trace) through a region using profile/branch probabilities, schedules it as if it were straight-line code moving instructions across side entrances/exits, and inserts **bookkeeping/compensation code** off-trace to preserve semantics. Hwu et al.'s **superblock scheduling** removes side *entrances* via **tail duplication**, leaving single-entry multiple-exit regions that need no entry compensation; **hyperblock** formation (Mahlke) adds if-conversion/predication to merge multiple paths for predicated architectures (IA-64). These are the global-scheduling mechanisms that feed ILP on wide-issue/VLIW machines.

**Software pipelining — modulo scheduling.** Rau's **iterative modulo scheduling** overlaps loop iterations at a fixed **initiation interval (II)**: compute lower bounds ResMII (resource-constrained) and RecMII (recurrence-constrained, from dependence cycles via max cycle-ratio), then attempt to place operations in a flat schedule modulo II with backtracking/eviction, incrementing II on failure. Resulting kernel needs **prologue/epilogue** generation and **modulo variable expansion** or **rotating register files** (Itanium) to resolve overlapping lifetimes. **Swing Modulo Scheduling** (Llosa et al.) is the register-pressure-aware variant ordering nodes to minimize lifetime, implemented in LLVM's MachinePipeliner (used for Hexagon, PowerPC). Supporting named ideas: **superscalar vs. VLIW hazard models**, **delay-slot filling** (historic MIPS/SPARC), and **anti-dependence breaking via register renaming** in the post-RA scheduler.

## 8. Loop Optimizations

**Loop-invariant code motion (LICM) and related motion.** Hoist computations whose operands are invariant in the loop to a **preheader** (and sink to exits), legal when the instruction dominates all exits or is speculatable; for memory, **promotion of loads/stores to scalars** (register promotion) requires alias-set analysis (LLVM AliasSetTracker / MemorySSA-based LICM) proving the location is not clobbered, with **store sinking** into exit blocks guarded by versioning when needed. The lattice-theoretic generalization is **Partial Redundancy Elimination** — Morel–Renvoise, modernized as Knoop–Rüthing–Steffen's **Lazy Code Motion** and SSA-based **GVN-PRE** — which subsumes LICM by making loop-invariants merely "partially redundant" along the back edge.

**Strength reduction and induction-variable optimization.** Classical **operator strength reduction** on induction variables (Allen–Cocke–Kennedy; Cooper–Simpson–Vick's SSA-based OSR) rewrites `i*c` recurrences as additive updates; modern compilers subsume this in **scalar evolution (SCEV)**-driven frameworks: LLVM's **IndVarSimplify** (canonicalize IVs, widen to eliminate sign/zero extensions, rewrite exit conditions via trip-count computation) and **Loop Strength Reduce (LSR)**, which formulates IV selection as choosing formulae minimizing register pressure and addressing-mode cost (crucial for targets with reg+imm or auto-increment addressing). **Linear function test replacement** eliminates the original IV when comparisons can be rewritten.

**Unrolling, fusion/distribution, interchange, tiling, and unswitching.** (a) **Loop unrolling** — full unrolling for constant trip counts, partial unrolling with epilogue/remainder or **runtime unrolling** with trip-count checks, plus **unroll-and-jam** for outer loops to expose ILP and reuse; cost-modeled against I-cache. (b) **Loop fusion** merges conforming adjacent loops to improve temporal locality and reduce loop overhead (legal if no fusion-preventing negative-distance dependences); its inverse **loop distribution/fission** splits a loop to isolate vectorizable SCCs or reduce register pressure. (c) **Loop interchange** permutes nest order for stride-1 access/vectorizability, legality via direction vectors. (d) **Loop tiling/blocking** (with the polyhedral model — Polly/Pluto's cost-function-driven affine scheduling and ISL code generation — as the general framework) partitions iteration spaces into cache-sized blocks; **skewing** enables tiling of stencils (time-tiling). (e) **Loop unswitching** hoists a loop-invariant conditional out, cloning the loop per branch arm (LLVM SimpleLoopUnswitch, including non-trivial unswitching); related **loop versioning** clones under runtime predicates (alias, alignment, unit-stride). Also properly in this family: **loop rotation** (to do-while form, enabling LICM/latch-exit canonicalization), **loop idiom recognition** (memset/memcpy/popcount formation), **loop peeling**, and **loop deletion** of dead loops via trip-count/side-effect proofs.

---

All eight areas above are covered with three or more specifically named, standard mechanisms each, with their governing data structures (dominance frontiers, interference graphs, connection graphs, dependence graphs, DDGs, SCEV), key authors/algorithm names (Cytron, Lengauer–Tarjan, Braun; Andersen, Steensgaard, TBAA; Chaitin–Briggs, linear scan/Greedy, Hack chordal/PBQP; cost-model inlining, partial inlining, speculative devirtualization/PIC; Choi connection graphs, partial escape analysis, Go's analysis; Allen–Kennedy, VPlan loop vectorizer, SLP; list scheduling, trace/superblock scheduling, modulo scheduling; LICM/PRE, strength reduction/LSR, unrolling–fusion–interchange–tiling–unswitching), and the legality and cost-model conditions under which each applies.

Answer: The technical brief above covers all eight requested areas — SSA construction (Cytron dominance-frontier construction with Lengauer–Tarjan/Cooper-Harvey-Kennedy dominators, pruned/semi-pruned SSA, Braun et al. on-the-fly construction with block arguments and SSA destruction), alias analysis (Andersen inclusion-based, Steensgaard unification-based, TBAA plus BasicAA/restrict and dependence tests), register allocation (Chaitin–Briggs graph coloring with iterated coalescing and rematerialization, linear scan/LLVM Greedy with live-range splitting, SSA-chordal and PBQP allocation), inlining (bottom-up cost-model inlining with PGO thresholds, partial inlining/function splitting and specialization, speculative devirtualization with polymorphic inline caches and deoptimization), escape analysis (Choi connection graphs, HotSpot/Graal partial escape analysis with scalar replacement, Go's assignment-graph analysis), loop vectorization (Allen–Kennedy dependence-based vectorization with if-conversion, LLVM VPlan vectorizer with runtime checks/masking/scalable vectors, SLP vectorization), instruction scheduling (list scheduling with machine models and pressure tracking, trace/superblock/hyperblock scheduling, iterative and swing modulo scheduling), and loop optimizations (LICM/lazy code motion/PRE, strength reduction with IndVarSimplify/LSR, and unrolling, fusion/distribution, interchange, tiling, unswitching, rotation, and idiom recognition) — each with at least three named mechanisms treated in depth using standard terminology.
